title: City Skyline
statement: A city planner draws the skyline of rectangular buildings standing on flat ground. Each building is [left, right, height] and covers x from left up to (not including) right. The skyline is described by key points [x, h]: at x the outline's height changes to h. Return the key points sorted by x, with no two consecutive points sharing the same height. The last key point always drops to height 0.

examples.explanation: The outline rises to 10, 15, then 12, drops to 0 at 12, rises to 10 at 15, 8 at 20 and 0 at 24.
Touching buildings of equal height merge into one flat stretch.

hints.content: The outline can only change at a building's left or right edge.
At each such x, the height is the tallest building with left <= x < right (0 if none).
Computing that maximum from scratch at every x is quadratic.
Sweep the x coordinates in order with a max-heap of (height, right) for buildings that have started.
At each x, push buildings that start there, lazily pop heap tops whose right <= x, read the top's height, and emit a key point only if it differs from the last one.

testCases.explanation: The outline rises to 10, 15, then 12, drops to 0 at 12, rises to 10 at 15, 8 at 20 and 0 at 24.
Touching buildings of equal height merge into one flat stretch.
One building: up at 1, down at 5.
Two towers on a long low building.
Duplicates and a taller building on the same footprint.
A gap drops to 0 between buildings.
A building hidden inside an equal-height one adds no key points; the outline steps down to 2 at 10.

solutions.title: Recompute the height at every edge
solutions.intuition: Evaluate the outline height at each candidate x directly.
solutions.approach: Collect all left and right coordinates, sort them, and for each x take the maximum height of buildings covering x. Emit a point whenever the height changes.
solutions.pseudocode: for x in sorted unique edges: h = max height with l <= x < r (or 0); if h != last: emit [x, h]
commonMistakes: Using x <= r, which keeps a building standing at its right edge.
Emitting a point at every edge even when the height does not change.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Every key point lies on an edge, so evaluating the height at each edge is correct. It scans all buildings for each of up to 2n edges, which is quadratic.

solutions.title: Sweep line with a lazy max-heap
solutions.intuition: Between edges the set of standing buildings is fixed, and a max-heap keyed by height exposes the tallest; ended buildings can be discarded only when they reach the top.
solutions.approach: Sort buildings by left and the unique edge coordinates. For each x: push (height, right) for buildings with left <= x; pop while the top's right <= x; height = top or 0; append [x, height] if it differs from the last point.
solutions.pseudocode:
for x in edges: push started buildings; while top.right <= x: pop
  h = top ? top.height : 0; if h != last: emit [x, h]
commonMistakes: Removing ended buildings from the middle of the heap eagerly, which is O(n) per removal; lazy deletion only removes them when they surface.
Popping ended buildings before pushing ones that start at the same x is fine; skipping the duplicate-height check is not.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The outline only changes at edges, so I sweep the sorted edges with a max-heap of standing buildings keyed by height. Buildings that have ended stay in the heap until they reach the top, where I discard them (lazy deletion), so each building is pushed and popped once, O(n log n) overall. I emit a key point only when the visible height changes, which also merges equal-height neighbors. A divide-and-conquer merge of skylines is the other classic O(n log n) approach.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: x=7: 15 ends → 12 → [7,12]. x=9: 10 ends, top still 12. x=12: all ended → [12,0].
